passage: The acceptance letter from the accounting firm in Osaka arrived on a Tuesday, and by Friday Hiroshi's father had booked a table at the family's favourite restaurant. It was the firm his father had talked about since Hiroshi was twelve. Hiroshi had studied for it for four years, turned down a summer at a pottery studio for it, practised the interviews in the mirror. Now, at the table, his uncles raised their glasses. Hiroshi smiled and raised his. Inside, he felt nothing. Not joy, not relief. Just a flat quiet, like a room after the guests have left. Later, walking home with his friend Thabo, he said, 'I thought I'd feel something.' Thabo asked, 'Did you want it, or did you want them to be happy?' Hiroshi didn't answer. He was thinking, oddly, about the smell of wet clay.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi turn down for the firm?
qa.a: He turned down a summer at a pottery studio.

qa.q: Why did Hiroshi feel nothing at the celebration?
qa.a: He had reached a goal set by his father, not one that matched his own values, so instead of joy he felt flat and empty.

qa.q: What could Hiroshi do with Thabo's question?
qa.a: He could reflect honestly on what he values, perhaps the pottery, and look for ways to bring it into his life and future choices.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi's father feel at the table?
qa.a: His father probably felt proud and joyful, seeing a long-held hope come true, unaware that Hiroshi felt empty.

grounding: A young man reaches the job his father always wanted for him and feels empty, because the goal was never his own.

passage: The convocation hall at the university in Jaipur was packed, and when they called 'Himani, gold medal, B.Sc. Chemistry', her parents stood up and cheered. Himani walked to the stage, bowed, and felt the medal settle on her neck. She had worked three years for this. Her mother had talked of the gold since the first semester; her friends had bet on it. Back in her seat, she waited for the happiness. It didn't come. Vasudha, beside her, squeezed her hand. 'You did it!' 'I did,' Himani said. She looked at the medal. It looked like someone else's. What she kept remembering, strangely, was last summer's volunteering at the village school, teaching children to grow bean sprouts in cotton wool, and how she had laughed all day. 'Why do I feel so empty?' she whispered. Vasudha didn't know what to say.

qa.q: What medal did Himani receive?
qa.a: She received the gold medal in B.Sc. Chemistry.

qa.q: Why did Himani feel empty after winning the gold medal?
qa.a: The gold was her mother's and friends' goal, not one tied to what she truly values, so achieving it brought little satisfaction.

qa.q: What might Himani learn from remembering the village school?
qa.a: That teaching children brought her real joy, so she could explore goals built around that rather than borrowed targets.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel hearing 'Why do I feel so empty?'
qa.a: Vasudha is likely confused and a little worried, since she expected her friend to be thrilled.

grounding: A student wins the gold medal her family and friends expected and feels empty, because the goal did not match her own values.

passage:
Dear Pema,
I cleared it. The state services prelims, first attempt. Everyone at home has been calling since morning. Papa distributed sweets in the whole lane. My friends from coaching say I'm a legend.
And I'm sitting here in my room feeling like I've climbed the wrong hill.
You know I only started this because everyone in our town said a government job is the only real success. My cousins, my coaching group, Papa. I never really asked myself what I wanted. I just ran. Now that I've arrived, it's quiet. No fireworks inside.
The only time this year I felt truly alive was the week I helped the NGO map the lake's birds. You were there. You saw.
I don't know what to do with this. Tell me honestly if I'm being ungrateful.
Naveen

qa.q: Which exam did Naveen clear?
qa.a: Naveen cleared the state services prelims, first attempt.

qa.q: What does Naveen mean by 'climbed the wrong hill'?
qa.a: Naveen feels empty and confused, because the goal came from the town, family and friends rather than from Naveen's own values.

qa.q: How could Pema help Naveen think this through?
qa.a: Pema could reassure Naveen that the feeling isn't ingratitude and help explore what the bird-mapping week says about what Naveen truly values.

qa.q: How does Papa experience the result?
qa.a: Papa is proud and joyful, distributing sweets in the lane, likely unaware of how Naveen feels inside.

grounding: In a letter, a young adult who cleared an exam chosen by family and friends describes feeling empty after reaching it.

passage: I share a flat with Vijay in Pune, so I've watched his half-marathon plan up close. In January he wrote one line on the fridge: Run 21 km in the city marathon, December. Under it he broke it down: January, walk-run 3 km. February, 5 km. Each Sunday evening he sat with a cup of tea and his notebook and reviewed the week. When he missed four runs in March because of a fever, I expected him to scrap the whole thing. He didn't. He crossed out March, wrote 'fever, rest', and moved the 8 km target to April. No drama. I can't say what he felt, but he hummed while he did it. In August, when the monsoon flooded his usual route, he switched to stair runs in our building. In December I stood at the 18 km mark with a banana. He waved it off. 'Uday,' he shouted, 'save it for the finish!'

qa.q: What did Vijay write on the fridge in January?
qa.a: He wrote: Run 21 km in the city marathon, December.

qa.q: What does Vijay humming while rescheduling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt calm and unbothered by the setback, treating the plan kindly rather than as a failure.

qa.q: Why did Vijay's weekly review help the plan survive?
qa.a: Reviewing kindly each Sunday let him adjust targets after the fever and the flooded route, so the big aim stayed alive.

qa.q: How did Uday expect Vijay to react to the fever?
qa.a: Uday expected the whole plan to be scrapped, and was surprised Vijay simply moved the target.

grounding: A flatmate describes an adult who splits a year-long running aim into monthly steps, reviews it kindly each week, and adapts to setbacks.

passage:
January. Kavitha wrote her aim on the first page of a new notebook: finish my children's book by December. Underneath: January, outline. February, three chapters. Every Sunday: one hour of writing, fifteen minutes reviewing the week, no scolding. Deepika, her roommate, raised an eyebrow. 'No scolding?'
April. Work had exploded, and Kavitha had written nothing for three weeks. On Sunday she opened the notebook, looked at the empty weeks, and wrote: 'Busy season. Not a failure. May: one page a week.' Then she wrote one page.
December. Deepika found the printed manuscript on the dining table, a little late, with a sticky note: Draft done, 29th. Kavitha was asleep on the sofa, pen still in her hand.

qa.q: What was Kavitha's aim?
qa.a: Her aim was to finish her children's book by December.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel in April, and how did she treat herself?
qa.a: She was likely disappointed after three blank weeks, but she wrote 'Not a failure', choosing kindness over scolding.

qa.q: What made Kavitha's plan survive the busy season?
qa.a: Weekly reviews without scolding let her shrink the target to one page a week instead of giving up, keeping the big aim alive.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel finding the manuscript?
qa.a: Deepika would likely feel impressed and happy, remembering her doubt about the 'no scolding' rule.

grounding: Over a year, an adult splits a big writing aim into monthly and weekly steps and reviews it kindly, so the plan survives a busy season.

passage: Akash, you want to open your own repair workshop, and you're frustrated because it hasn't happened in six months. Let me tell you how I did mine, back when I was twenty-five and fixing motors for someone else. My big aim was simple: my own shop by thirty. I wrote it on the wall behind my bed. Then my wife made me do the boring part. Every month, one step. Get my licence. Learn accounts at night school. Find a used lathe. And every Sunday we sat with tea and asked: what did I do this week, and what's next? Some Sundays the answer was 'nothing, I was tired'. We didn't shout. We just made the next week smaller. The lathe took a year longer than planned. The shop opened when I was thirty-one. Your Naveen Mama is still proud of that one year's delay.

qa.q: What was Naveen's big aim?
qa.a: Naveen's aim was his own shop by thirty.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel on Sundays when the answer was 'nothing'?
qa.a: Naveen was probably disappointed and tired, but the calm, no-shouting review let him feel steady enough to make the next week smaller.

qa.q: What choice in the story kept Naveen's aim alive?
qa.a: Breaking the aim into monthly steps and reviewing kindly each Sunday, shrinking targets when needed instead of giving up.

qa.q: How might Naveen's wife have seen the weekly reviews?
qa.a: She likely saw them as a way to keep his dream practical and gentle, which is why she insisted on the 'boring part'.

grounding: An uncle recalls splitting his aim of owning a workshop into monthly steps with kind weekly reviews, a flexible plan that survived delays.

passage: Last year I only did the jigsaw puzzles I already knew. The farm one, the train one, the jungle one. I could finish each in ten minutes, and I felt clever. When Kavitha Ma'am brought a new puzzle of a city at night, all dark blue pieces, I said I had a headache. I didn't. I was scared I'd get it wrong in front of everyone. So I did the farm puzzle again, for the fifth time. My friend tried the city one, got stuck, and laughed about it. I didn't laugh. I just watched. Kavitha Ma'am asked, 'Parveen, don't you want to try something new?' I said the farm one was more fun. It wasn't. I just knew I couldn't be wrong at it.

qa.q: What was the new puzzle Kavitha Ma'am brought?
qa.a: It was a city at night, with all dark blue pieces.

qa.q: Why did Parveen say there was a headache?
qa.a: Parveen was scared of getting the new puzzle wrong in front of everyone, so pretending to be unwell felt safer.

qa.q: How could Kavitha Ma'am help Parveen try the new puzzle?
qa.a: Kavitha Ma'am could invite Parveen to do one small corner with a friend, and show that getting stuck is a normal part of learning.

qa.q: How did Parveen's friend handle getting stuck?
qa.a: The friend got stuck and laughed about it, showing that being wrong didn't feel scary.

grounding: A child who fears being wrong looks back on doing only familiar puzzles and avoiding a new one, which felt safe but blocked learning.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Thursday.
Mehak is quick and neat, and loves finishing first. But she only picks worksheets she has done before. Today I put out a new kind of puzzle, number pyramids, where you guess and check. Mehak looked at it, went pale, and asked if she could do the old addition sheet instead. When I said everyone was trying pyramids, she wrote one number, rubbed it out so hard the paper tore, and sat still with her hands in her lap. She told me quietly, 'What if it's wrong?' I said wrong answers are how we find the right ones, and showed her my own crossed-out tries on the board. She tried one more number. Plan: next week I'll give her 'mistake-friendly' puzzles in pairs and praise her tries, not only her answers.
Indu

qa.q: What new kind of puzzle did the teacher put out?
qa.a: The teacher put out number pyramids.

qa.q: Why did Mehak rub out her number so hard the paper tore?
qa.a: She was anxious and afraid of being wrong, so she couldn't bear leaving a guess that might not be right.

qa.q: What plan will help Mehak try new things?
qa.a: Pairing her for 'mistake-friendly' puzzles and praising her tries, not only her answers.

qa.q: How might Indu feel watching Mehak sit still?
qa.a: Indu likely felt concerned and gentle, which is why the crossed-out tries on the board were shown to her.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a child who fears being wrong clinging to familiar worksheets and avoiding a new kind of puzzle.

passage:
Saturday
Chess club today. Jeevan wanted to teach me a new opening, the one where you move the horse first. I said no, I'll just do my usual one. My usual one always works, and nobody can say I did it wrong. He said I'll never get better if I only play the same way. I said I don't care. Then I played the same opening four times and won twice and lost twice, the same as always.
When I got home I watched Jeevan's opening on Papa's phone. It looked interesting. But what if I try it at club and lose in six moves and everyone sees? That would be so embarrassing.
Maybe I'll practise it with Papa first, where nobody can see.
Farida

qa.q: Which piece does Jeevan's new opening move first?
qa.a: It moves the horse first.

qa.q: Why does Farida keep playing the usual opening?
qa.a: Farida is afraid of being wrong or embarrassed in front of others, so the familiar opening feels safe even though it keeps Farida stuck.

qa.q: Is practising with Papa first a good idea, and why?
qa.a: Yes; trying the new opening where mistakes feel safe is a small step toward learning without the fear of being seen losing.

qa.q: How does Jeevan see Farida's choice?
qa.a: Jeevan thinks Farida will never improve by always playing the same way, and seems frustrated at the refusal to try.

grounding: A child who fears losing in front of others sticks to a familiar chess opening, which feels safe but blocks learning.

passage: The block-level quiz final was held in the panchayat hall in Tirur, and Ayesha's team lost on the last question because she pressed the buzzer too early and said Kolkata instead of Chennai. The whole hall groaned. She kept her face still until she got home, then locked herself in the bathroom. For a week she didn't go near the school library, where the quiz team met. When the notice for the district quiz went up, her brother Jeevan brought it home. 'Your team's asking for you.' 'They're better off without me. I'm the one who lost it.' 'You also got them to the final.' Ayesha shook her head. It didn't feel like that. It felt as if the whole hall had seen who she really was: someone who panics and ruins things.

qa.q: What did Ayesha say instead of Chennai?
qa.a: She said Kolkata instead of Chennai.

qa.q: Why does Ayesha avoid the quiz team for a week?
qa.a: She feels deeply ashamed, as if one wrong answer showed the whole hall who she really is, so facing the team feels unbearable.

qa.q: What could help Ayesha return to the quiz?
qa.a: Remembering she got the team to the final, and talking with her teammates, who are asking for her, could show that one mistake isn't her worth.

qa.q: How do Ayesha's teammates seem to see her?
qa.a: They still want her for the district quiz, which suggests they value her far more than she believes.

grounding: A teenager who lost a quiz final with one wrong answer feels her worth has fallen and avoids the next contest.

passage: After Clara's team lost the regional debate final in Adelaide, she read the judges' sheet on the bus home: 'Clara's rebuttal lacked structure.' She read it until the words blurred. At school on Monday she avoided the debate room. When Mei told her the Model UN sign-ups closed on Friday, Clara said she was too busy. 'You love Model UN.' 'I'm just not good at that kind of thing,' Clara said. 'Clearly.' 'Because of one sheet?' Clara didn't answer. It wasn't the sheet. It was the moment she'd stood up, lost her place, and seen the judge write something down. In her head that moment had become a label: someone who falls apart. Friday came. Clara walked past the sign-up table twice and kept walking.

qa.q: What did the judges' sheet say about Clara's rebuttal?
qa.a: It said her rebuttal lacked structure.

qa.q: Why did Clara walk past the sign-up table twice?
qa.a: She felt ashamed after the loss and feared another failure would prove she is 'someone who falls apart', so avoiding the contest felt safer.

qa.q: What could Clara do instead of avoiding Model UN?
qa.a: Sign up and work on one specific skill, like structuring rebuttals, treating the feedback as something to fix rather than a label.

qa.q: How might Mei feel watching Clara skip the sign-ups?
qa.a: Mei would likely feel sad and puzzled, since she knows how much Clara loves Model UN.

grounding: A teenager who lost a debate final treats the loss as proof of who she is and avoids the next contest.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta Baji,
You asked which electives I finally picked. I went with Office Management and Basic Statistics. Easy A's, everyone says. My CGPA is 9.1, and I want to keep it above 9 for master's applications.
You'll ask about astrophysics. Yes, it was open. Yes, I've wanted it since I was ten and you took me to the planetarium. But the seniors say the professor is tough and half the class gets B's. One B could drop me to 8.8. I couldn't risk it.
I keep telling myself it's the smart move. But when I walked past the astrophysics lecture hall yesterday and saw the star charts on the wall, I felt as if I'd sold something I can't get back.
Is this what growing up is? Playing safe?
Hafsa

qa.a: Hafsa's CGPA is 9.1.

qa.q: How did Hafsa feel walking past the astrophysics hall?
qa.a: Hafsa felt a pang of loss and regret, as if something precious had been traded away for a safe grade.

qa.q: What could Hafsa do to act less from fear?
qa.a: Hafsa could weigh the real cost of one B against years of wanting astrophysics, and talk with the professor or a mentor before the change deadline.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Baji feel reading this?
qa.a: Sangeeta Baji would likely feel sad and protective, remembering the planetarium trip and not wanting a younger cousin to give up the dream for a number.

grounding: In a letter, a student describes picking easy electives to protect a high grade average and skipping the field they love.

passage: Anand, you asked why I wanted a podcast episode about playing it safe. So here's mine. I'm Ritu, final year B.Com, 8.7 CGPA. In first year I had a choice: a music minor, which I've loved since I was seven, or accounting electives. Everyone said the music professor marks hard. So I picked accounting. Safe. Every semester, same choice, same reason. My grades are lovely. I'm on track for a good job. And I haven't touched my harmonium in two years, because every time I open it, I remember I chose not to try. It wasn't really the grades making the choice. It was fear. Fear that if I tried music properly and wasn't good enough, I'd lose the one thing I thought I was good at. So I never found out. That's the part that stings.

qa.q: How long has Ritu not touched the harmonium?
qa.a: Ritu hasn't touched it in two years.

qa.q: Which feeling does Ritu say was really making the choices?
qa.a: Fear: fear of trying music properly and not being good enough, which seemed likely to take away the one thing Ritu felt good at.

qa.q: What could Ritu try now, even in final year?
qa.a: Ritu could take a short music course or lessons without grades, trying the music Ritu loves without pressure on the CGPA.

qa.q: How might Anand respond to Ritu's story?
qa.a: Anand might feel moved and relate to it, since the episode is about how people quietly choose safety over what they love.

grounding: A final-year student describes choosing safe courses every semester to protect grades, never trying the music they love.

passage:
Registration day. Vidya's cursor hovered over Marine Biology for a full minute. The seniors said the professor failed a third of the class. She clicked Environmental Awareness instead: guaranteed A, no fieldwork. Her CGPA would stay above 9.

passage:
Dear Gautam Sir,
You told me to write this down when the kitchen closed, so here it is, six weeks late.
The tiffin service lasted nine months. Here is what I learned. One: I priced for my friends, not for my costs. Two: I tried to cook eight dishes; the two that sold were the only ones I should have made. Three: I did the deliveries myself and had no time left to find office clients. Four: I didn't ask anyone for help until it was too late.
I've told Ammi and my friend Rukhsar all of this too. Saying it out loud made it smaller.
For the next attempt I'm starting with two dishes, three offices, and a delivery partner from day one. I'd love fifteen minutes of your time to check my numbers before I begin.
It still hurts. But it doesn't feel like the end.
Ayesha

qa.q: How long did the tiffin service last?
qa.a: It lasted nine months.

qa.q: What does Ayesha mean by 'Saying it out loud made it smaller'?
qa.a: Sharing the failure with trusted people eased Ayesha's shame, so it felt like something to learn from rather than a crushing verdict.

qa.q: How is Ayesha applying the lessons to the next attempt?
qa.a: By starting with two dishes, three offices and a delivery partner from day one, and asking Gautam Sir to check the numbers first.

qa.q: How might Gautam Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Gautam Sir would likely feel proud and encouraged that Ayesha turned a painful failure into clear lessons.

grounding: In a letter to a mentor, an adult whose food business failed lists the lessons learned, shares them with trusted people, and applies them to the next attempt.

passage: Thanks, Elizabeth. Hi, everyone, I'm Gurpreet, and two years ago my bicycle rental for tourists in Amritsar shut down after eleven months. For a few weeks I didn't tell anyone. I thought failing meant I was a failure. Then my father sat me down and said, 'Write it like a mechanic's report. What broke, and why?' So I did. Winters killed demand; I'd planned for summer only. My shop was near the temple, but tourists walked there anyway. And I did everything alone. I read that report to three people I trust: my father, my old boss, and my friend who runs a café. Each one added something I'd missed. My new business, walking food tours, runs all year, starts where tourists already walk, and I have a partner. Last month we broke even. The first attempt wasn't wasted. It was the first draft.

qa.q: How long did the bicycle rental last?
qa.a: It lasted eleven months.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel in the first weeks after the shutdown?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt ashamed and kept it hidden, believing that failing meant being a failure.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that turned failure into data?
qa.a: Wrote a 'mechanic's report' of what broke, shared it with three trusted people, and applied each lesson to the new food-tour business.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's father have seen the failure?
qa.a: Gurpreet's father likely saw it as something to examine and learn from, not a judgement on Gurpreet, which is why he suggested the mechanic's report.

grounding: An adult tells a meetup how a failed rental business became lessons written down, shared with trusted people, and applied to a new venture.

passage: I've known Karthik since engineering college, so I was there when his tuition-booking startup shut down last spring after a year and a half. I expected him to disappear for a while. He did, for about two weeks. Then he called me and two others to his flat, put a whiteboard in the middle of the room, and wrote: WHAT I LEARNED. He listed things without defending himself: built features before talking to parents; hired too fast; ignored the numbers in month six. I don't know exactly what it cost him to write that; his voice was flat and he kept rubbing his neck. He asked each of us to add one thing he'd missed. I said he never took a weekend off. He wrote that down too. His new project, a small tutoring service for three schools, started with forty parent interviews. It's growing slowly. 'Seema,' he told me last week, 'version one paid for version two's lessons.'

qa.q: What did Karthik write at the top of the whiteboard?
qa.a: He wrote WHAT I LEARNED.

qa.q: What does Karthik's flat voice and neck-rubbing suggest?
qa.a: It suggests writing down his failures was uncomfortable and painful, even as he chose to face them.

qa.q: How did Karthik use the failure as data?
qa.a: He listed lessons honestly, asked trusted friends to add what he'd missed, and started the new project with forty parent interviews.

qa.q: How did Seema expect Karthik to react?
qa.a: Seema expected him to disappear for a while, and was struck by how openly he examined what went wrong.

grounding: A friend describes an adult whose startup failed writing down its lessons, inviting trusted people to add to them, and using them in his next project.

passage: In Class 4, I used to watch Sharmila Miss's face instead of the question. If she asked, 'Is a whale a fish?' I'd say 'Yes,' then see her eyebrows go up, and quickly say, 'No! Mammal!' Her face would relax, and I'd feel warm all over. Once she asked what I thought of a poem, and I waited to see if she smiled or frowned before I answered. She did neither. She just waited. I got so nervous I said, 'It's nice,' which isn't a thought at all. Afterwards she said, 'Thomas, I want to know what you think, not what you think I think.' I didn't understand then. I do a bit more now.

qa.q: What did Thomas first say when asked if a whale is a fish?
qa.a: Thomas first said 'Yes'.

qa.q: Why did Thomas watch Sharmila Miss's face instead of the question?
qa.a: Thomas felt anxious for her approval, and her pleased face brought a warm feeling, so pleasing her mattered more than thinking independently.

qa.q: What was helpful about Sharmila Miss waiting without reacting?
qa.a: It left space for Thomas's own thought instead of a guess about her face, nudging toward honest answers.

qa.q: What does Sharmila Miss want from Thomas?
qa.a: She wants to hear Thomas's own thoughts, not answers shaped to please her.

grounding: A child looks back on changing answers to match the teacher's face, as the wish for approval crowded out honest thought.

passage:
Class 3 teacher's note, Monday.
Gargi is a lovely, eager child, but I've noticed something this term. When I ask a question, she answers, then watches my face and changes her answer if I pause. Today in science I asked whether a plant needs sunlight. She said yes, I paused to write on the board, and she said, 'No, I mean no,' then, 'Yes?' She looked close to tears. Later, when the class drew their own idea of a rainforest, she kept asking, 'Is this right? Is this how you want it?' I told her there is no one right rainforest and I wanted to see hers. She drew for a while, then stopped and waited for me to come and nod. Plan: keep my face neutral during answers, praise her reasons rather than her right answers, and talk to her parents about how she is at home.
Usha

qa.q: What did the teacher ask the class to draw?
qa.a: The class drew their own idea of a rainforest.

qa.q: Why did Gargi change her answer when the teacher paused?
qa.a: She was anxious to please and read the pause as disapproval, so she switched answers to win approval, looking close to tears.

qa.q: What plan might help Gargi think for herself?
qa.a: Keeping a neutral face during answers, praising her reasons rather than right answers, and talking with her parents.

qa.q: How might Usha feel watching Gargi wait for a nod?
qa.a: Usha likely feels concerned and tender, wanting Gargi to trust her own ideas.

grounding: A teacher's note describes a child who changes answers and watches faces anxiously for signs of approval, crowding out her own thinking.

passage:
Tuesday
Nirmala Ma'am asked us to write whether school uniforms are good or bad. I actually think they're bad, because they're hot and I can't wear my yellow kurta. But in class Ma'am said uniforms make everyone equal, and she smiled when she said it. So I wrote that uniforms are good. Three paragraphs about equality. I didn't believe any of them.
When she handed the essays back, she'd written 'Very good, Arohi!' and I felt happy for about a minute. Then I felt strange, like the 'very good' was for somebody else.
Pihu wrote that uniforms are bad and gave real reasons. Ma'am wrote 'Strong argument!' on hers too. So she didn't even mind.
Next time I'm going to write what I think. Probably.

qa.q: What does Arohi actually think about uniforms?
qa.a: Arohi thinks they're bad, because they're hot and the yellow kurta can't be worn.

qa.q: Why did the 'Very good' feel like it was for somebody else?
qa.a: Arohi wrote what seemed to please Ma'am, not what Arohi believed, so the praise brought brief happiness and then an uneasy, hollow feeling.

qa.q: What did Arohi learn from Pihu's essay?
qa.a: That Ma'am also praised a different, honest opinion, so Arohi could write real thoughts without losing approval.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Ma'am feel if she knew Arohi had written against Arohi's own view?
qa.a: She would likely feel concerned, since she praised Pihu's honest argument and seems to want real reasons, not agreement.

grounding: A child writes an essay to match the teacher's smile rather than her own view, and the praise feels hollow.

passage:
Dear Ira,
You asked how the new friends are. They're fun, mostly. Popular, too. I sit with them at lunch now.
But something's bugging me. Yesterday Neil made fun of Sameer's lunch, the upma his grandmother packs every day. He called it 'wet sand' and everyone laughed. I laughed too. I actually like upma. My Nani makes it. But I laughed louder than anyone, because I didn't want them to look at me the way they looked at Sameer.
Then Neil said the new history teacher is useless, and I agreed, even though I think she's the best one we've got.
I keep saying yes to everything they say. It's like I'm scared that if I disagree once, I'll be back to sitting alone. Is that stupid?
Write back.
Akash

qa.q: What does Sameer's grandmother pack every day?
qa.a: She packs upma every day.

qa.q: Why did Akash laugh louder than anyone?
qa.a: Akash was afraid of being rejected and ending up like Sameer, so pleasing the group mattered more than Akash's own view.

qa.q: What small step could Akash take to be more honest with the group?
qa.a: Akash could stop laughing at jokes that feel wrong, or quietly say upma is good, starting with one small disagreement.

qa.q: How might Sameer feel when everyone laughs at his lunch?
qa.a: Sameer would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, especially about food his grandmother makes for him.

grounding: In a letter, a teenager admits laughing at jokes they dislike and agreeing against their own view, out of fear of the group's rejection.

passage: Vasudha, you want to know why I called that film 'trash' at lunch when I told you last week it was the best thing I'd seen all year? Honestly? Because Karan said it first, and then everyone agreed, and I felt my mouth open and 'yeah, total trash' came out. I didn't even decide. It just came out. Same on Friday, when they decided to bunk the physics practical. I like physics practicals. I went with them anyway and sat behind the canteen feeling stupid. I think I'm scared that if I say 'actually, I liked it', they'll look at me the way they looked at the new boy when he said he doesn't watch cricket. As if he'd stopped existing. So I say yes. To everything. I'm Varun, and apparently I have no opinions anymore. Isn't that funny?

qa.q: What did Varun say about the film at lunch?
qa.a: He said, 'Yeah, total trash.'

qa.q: Why does Varun say yes to everything the group decides?
qa.a: He is afraid of being rejected and treated as if he'd stopped existing, like the new boy, so the group's approval matters more than his own views.

qa.q: What could Varun try next time the group disagrees with him?
qa.a: He could say one small honest thing, like 'I liked it', and see that disagreeing doesn't have to mean rejection.

qa.q: How might Vasudha feel hearing Varun called the film trash?
qa.a: Vasudha might feel confused and a little let down, since he had told her it was the best film he'd seen all year.

grounding: A teenager tells a friend how fear of rejection makes him echo the group, trashing a film he loved and skipping a class he enjoys.

passage:
Monday. When the group laughed at Anjali's poem in the school magazine, calling it 'so cringe', Baljeet laughed too. He had read it twice at home and liked it.
Wednesday. The class voted on the trip: the science museum or the water park. Baljeet had wanted the museum for months. The group all put their hands up for the water park, looking round to check. Baljeet raised his hand with them.
Friday. At home, Baljeet opened the school magazine and read Anjali's poem again. It was still good. He felt a heavy, sour feeling, as if he'd swallowed something wrong. He couldn't remember the last time he'd said what he actually thought in front of them. He wondered if they even knew what he liked.

qa.q: Which trip had Baljeet wanted for months?
qa.a: He had wanted the science museum.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet raise his hand for the water park?
qa.a: He feared standing out and being rejected, so matching the group felt safer than voting for what he wanted.

qa.q: What could Baljeet do to start being himself with the group?
qa.a: Start with a small honest moment, like telling Anjali he liked her poem, to see that disagreeing doesn't end friendships.

qa.q: How might Anjali feel hearing the group call her poem 'cringe'?
qa.a: Anjali would likely feel hurt and embarrassed, especially after sharing something personal in the magazine.

grounding: Over a week, a teenager laughs at a poem he liked and votes against his own wish to keep the group's approval.

passage: Every decision Jasleen made, she ran past her father first. Which elective, which kurta for the college fest, whether to cut her hair. Bhupen always had an answer, and his 'shabaash, puttar' felt like sunshine. So when the design firm in Bengaluru offered her a six-month internship, she didn't tell anyone for three days. She sat on the terrace of their house in Ludhiana with the email open on her phone, feeling sick. She wanted it more than anything. And she knew Papa's face would fall; he had always said she'd work in the family printing business after college. On the fourth day she brought him tea and said, 'Papa, I got an offer.' He read it slowly. He didn't say shabaash. He said, 'Bengaluru is very far.' That night Jasleen lay awake, torn between the offer and the guilt of wanting it.

qa.q: Where was the design firm that offered the internship?
qa.a: It was in Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen feel sick sitting on the terrace?
qa.a: She wanted the internship badly, but loved her father and felt guilty that her wish went against his plans, so love and duty pulled against each other.

qa.q: What could Jasleen do to honour both love and her own wish?
qa.a: She could talk openly with Papa about why the internship matters, ask about his worries, and look for a plan that respects both, such as returning after six months.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel reading the email?
qa.a: Bhupen probably felt worried and a little sad, imagining his daughter far away and his hopes for the family business changing.

grounding: A young woman who seeks her father's praise for every decision feels guilty wanting an internship that goes against his plans.

passage:
'You're calling your dad again?' Rafiq said from the top bunk. 'For a club?'
Omkar hung up. 'He said theatre's a waste of time. He wants me in the robotics club.'
'Do you want robotics?'
'No. But Baba's sacrificed so much. He drove me here himself. He calls every night.'
'So you'll do robotics.'
'I don't know.' Omkar sat on his bed. 'Every time I think about theatre, I feel guilty. Like I'm betraying him.'
'Or like you're growing up?'
'He'd be so proud if I did robotics.'
'And you'd be miserable.'
Omkar laughed a little. 'That's the problem. I want him to be proud. And I want to be me.'
'Can't he be proud of you in a play?'
'I've never asked him.'
Rafiq threw a pillow at him. 'Then maybe start there.'

qa.q: Which club does Omkar's father want him to join?
qa.a: He wants Omkar in the robotics club.

qa.q: Why does Omkar feel like he's betraying his father?
qa.a: He loves his father and wants his pride, so wanting theatre instead makes him feel guilty, as if his own wish were disloyal.

qa.q: What does Rafiq suggest Omkar do?
qa.a: Ask his father whether he could be proud of Omkar in a play, instead of assuming robotics is the only way to please him.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Omkar's dilemma?
qa.a: Rafiq sees it as part of growing up and wants Omkar to talk to his father rather than give up what he wants.

grounding: A young man who seeks his father's approval for every choice feels guilty wanting theatre instead of the club his father prefers.

passage: Until last year I had never made a decision without asking Amma first. Not which shoes, not which friends, not which college. Her smile was the thing I worked for. So when I realised I wanted to switch from chartered accountancy to journalism, I couldn't sleep for a week. Amma had framed my CA foundation certificate. She'd told every relative. Every time I imagined telling her, I felt a thick guilt in my throat, as if wanting something for myself were a kind of stealing. When I finally told her over Sunday lunch, she went very quiet. Then she said, 'Ujjwal, I wanted you safe. I didn't know you were unhappy.' She didn't say yes that day. But she didn't say no either. Now I'm in my first semester of journalism, and she still calls every evening. Some days I still check her face before I choose anything. I'm learning not to.

qa.q: What had Amma framed?
qa.a: She had framed Ujjwal's CA foundation certificate.

qa.q: Why did wanting journalism feel 'like stealing' to Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ujjwal loved Amma and depended on her approval, so wanting something different brought a thick sense of guilt, as if taking something from her.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal move forward?
qa.a: Telling Amma honestly over lunch, which let her explain that she wanted Ujjwal safe and hadn't known about the unhappiness.

qa.q: How did Amma respond to the news?
qa.a: She went quiet, explained she had wanted Ujjwal safe and hadn't known about the unhappiness, and neither agreed nor refused that day.

grounding: A young adult from a close family looks back on needing a mother's approval for every choice and the guilt of wanting a different career.

passage: At the architecture office in Copenhagen, Emil noticed that whenever anyone asked Layla for anything, the answer was yes. Could she review the drawings? Yes. Could she cover Friday's site visit? Yes. Could she organise the summer party? Of course. Lately she ate lunch at her desk, her eyes were red by four, and once he found her asleep in the meeting room at seven in the evening. On Thursday the project manager asked her to take on the museum proposal too. Layla opened her mouth, and Emil could almost hear the yes coming. He cut in. 'Actually, I've got space this week. I can take the museum proposal, with Layla checking one section.' Later, by the coffee machine, he said quietly, 'You can say no. If it helps, say "Let me check with Emil" and I'll back you up.' Layla laughed, surprised, and then her eyes filled. 'I don't know how,' she said.

qa.q: Where did Emil once find Layla asleep?
qa.a: He found her asleep in the meeting room at seven in the evening.

qa.q: What was Emil feeling when he cut in?
qa.a: Emil felt concerned and protective, seeing her exhaustion and sensing another automatic yes was coming.

qa.q: What backup did Emil offer Layla?
qa.a: He took part of the museum proposal himself and gave her a phrase, 'Let me check with Emil', so she could practise saying no without losing standing.

qa.q: Why might Layla's eyes fill when Emil says she can say no?
qa.a: Layla is probably exhausted and relieved, and it may be the first time someone noticed how hard it is for her to refuse.

grounding: A colleague notices a teammate who agrees to every request and is burning out, and offers backup so she can practise saying no.

passage: In the school staffroom, the duty roster went up every Monday, and every Monday there was a new line with Leela's name on it. Exam invigilation, annual day costumes, the science club, and now the principal was asking whether she would also take the Class 6 remedial group. Charu, who shared a table with her, watched Leela nod before the sentence had even ended. She had seen Leela marking papers in the car park at eight at night, and heard her cancel her own dentist appointment twice. Charu waited until the principal left. 'Leela, I'll say it once. You're allowed to say no.' Leela gave a tired laugh. 'If I say no, they'll think I'm not a team player.' 'Then let's practise. Next time, say you'll check your load and come back. I'll back you up in the meeting.' On Friday, when a new request came, Leela said, 'Let me check my load.' Charu gave her a tiny nod across the room.

qa.q: What new group was the principal asking Leela to take?
qa.a: The Class 6 remedial group.

qa.q: What did Charu feel watching Leela nod before the sentence ended?
qa.a: Charu felt worried and a little frustrated, having seen Leela marking at night and cancelling her own appointments.

qa.q: How did Charu help Leela practise saying no?
qa.a: She gave Leela a simple phrase, 'Let me check my load', and promised to back her up in meetings.

qa.q: Why does Leela find it hard to say no?
qa.a: Leela fears being seen as not a team player, so agreeing to everything feels safer than risking disapproval.

grounding: A teacher notices a colleague agreeing to every duty and quietly burning out, and offers backup so she can practise saying no.

passage:
Subject: A slightly awkward email from your desk neighbour

Himani,
I've been meaning to say this in person, but I keep chickening out, so here it is.
Over the last two months I've watched you say yes to everything: the client audit, the intern training, Rajiv's reports when he was on leave, the Diwali event. You've stayed till ten most nights. Yesterday you said, 'I'm fine,' and then fell asleep during the review.
I don't think anyone expects you to do all of it. I think they ask because you always say yes.
So here's an offer. Next time someone brings you something new, you can say, 'Let me check with Ramesh; we're sharing that workload.' I'll back you up, and I'll actually take some of it. You won't look like you're refusing; you'll look organised.
Practise on me first if you like. Say no to my next request.
Ramesh

qa.q: What happened during yesterday's review?
qa.a: Himani fell asleep during the review.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh keep 'chickening out' of saying this in person?
qa.a: Ramesh felt awkward and worried about upsetting Himani, even though the concern about Himani's exhaustion was strong.

qa.q: What does Ramesh offer to help Himani say no?
qa.a: A phrase, 'Let me check with Ramesh', real backup, and a promise to take some of the work, so refusing won't hurt Himani's standing.

qa.q: Why might Himani keep saying yes to everything?
qa.a: Himani may fear disappointing people or losing standing, so agreeing feels safer than refusing, even while burning out.

grounding: In an email, a colleague who has watched a teammate say yes to everything offers backup so the teammate can practise saying no.
